Nice Jig

This is a very pretty tune that I do not get to play very often. I would like to share with everyone. This setting is very close to traditional Sligo setting as well as to the “Old” O’Neill’s (1907).

Slight variation

I usually play section 3 different, I like this version a LOT more, try it yourself: (I have not tested this ABC, I may have a note length wrong or something sorry)

|: B | efe fdB | def g2 a | fdd add | fag fed | gfg efe | dfe ggg | edB BAF | GDD D2 :|

In addition, this song is in e minor and should end on an E not on a G, though the G does sound interesting.

Often, when there is a situation where there is a triplet that starts on one not eand falls to another and stays there for the third, I play the second two as their own mini-triplet. I forget the term. On low-whistle. Sounds nice.

Also very pretty when played quite slow.

Tony MacMahon version

My favorite version of this is the one played by Tony MacMahon. Perhaps the recording I had was wonky but the playing was in F minor. I transcribed and transposed it to E minor. The transcription is not perfect - MacMahon frequently modifies the tune just a bit as he repeats sections - and I have made no attempt to capture any of the ornamentation but still enjoy playing this version:

The Old Gray Goose, X:6

Rónán Mac Grianna’s version. Great version, took me a while to get it all sorted out and written down but worthwhile - easy to forget it with all those parts! The transcripition is more or less based on the first time each section’s played first time through. There are quite a lot of variations but I left them out as it’d be too much of a muddle to write it all down. Some of the parts differ substantially when repeated and also each time the tune’s played. Ornamentation omitted for the same reasons. Great tune, might be becoming on of my favourites.

↳ Posted by Harry Emma on June 28th, 2015.

The Old Gray Goose, X:7

This tune – “a variant of The Old Grey Goose” says the Fiddler’s Companion – appears in P.W. Joyce’s Old Irish Music and Songs (1909), vol. 1, p. 113-114, No. 232, as The Rakes of Kinsale.
Joyce wrote that he copied it from two very old well-written manuscripts lent to him in 1873 by Mr J. O’Sullivan, of Bruff, Co. Limerick.

The Old Grey Goose, X:9

Basically copy and paste from version 5 with following changes inspired by Geraldine Cotter’s Traditional Irish Tin Whistle Tutor version :

Part B : I play c natural instead of C#. This c natural is found here and there in some version, while other setting play c#. I rather play c#
Part B : roll on A in bar 3 instead of A2 A

Part D : bar 3 : instead of repeating the bar 3 of schriltz’s setting, I play the bar 3 setting given by Geraldine Cotter in the second round. This gives a nice variation and I like both setting as well thus I have the two in the same tune.

↳ Posted by Helen Snibson on August 21st, 2024.

The Old Grey Goose, X:11 / S: Denis Murphy

Denis Murphy’s version of The Old Grey Goose recorded by Séamus Ennis at an unknown date and published by the Handed Down Sliabh Luachra Audio Archive in 2020.

https://on.soundcloud.com/TRieTMhhuHAUQWqk7

This is a great recording of Denis Murphy’s playing, including several duets with Séamus Ennis. My theory is that this reel-to-reel was recorded post-1965 after Denis Murphy’s return from the US – Ennis visited Murphy several times over the years and they also went on a couple of intense field trips together!

Check out the full tracklist of this tape on #ProjectDenis (search Collections for HD20):
https://sliabhluachra.github.io/ProjectDenis/

P.S.: Denis Murphy also played a slightly different two-part version of this tune which he called Geese in the Bog and associated with a song / verse that goes like this:

“My grandmother gave me a nice little job
Minding the geese in the foot of the bog.
The f[leeing] old gander he gave me a prod
& tis will I remember the geese in the bog.”

This verse comes from the Breandán Breathnach materials dated November 1970. Maybe someone knows an alternative version of this song!
